rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.

Injection 1 already attained the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient while keeping temperature and endpoints fixed to test whether its substantial resolution margin permits a faster fully resolved method.

Shorten the gradient another grid step to reduce analysis time while targeting the maximum CRF already achieved. The first pair remains the limiting separation, with resolution 2.68 providing room for further compression.
Test the minimum gradient duration to establish the speed–resolution boundary. The first pair may fall below 1.5; if so, the fully resolved 4-minute gradient remains the fallback.
Return to the shortest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature to test faster elution while retaining maximum CRF. This also measures temperature sensitivity of the critical first pair.
Back off one temperature step from 50 C to target first-pair resolution just above 1.5. This should modestly shorten elution relative to 40 C while potentially preserving the maximum CRF.

Lower temperature should improve selectivity of the critical early pair, while a slightly lower endpoint softens the gradient slope. Test whether these changes allow full resolution with a 2-minute gradient and faster final elution than injection 6.

Reduce the endpoint by one grid step to soften the gradient and lift the critical pair above its current resolution of 1.49. The last peak has ample time margin, so a modest delay should still permit maximum CRF with a faster separation than injection 6.

Shift both endpoints upward while preserving injection 8’s gradient slope, aiming to accelerate the last peak without losing full resolution. This tests whether the critical early pair tolerates a stronger starting solvent.

Shift the gradient window upward another step at the same slope to accelerate the last peak. Injection 9 preserved first-pair resolution, suggesting this shift may retain maximum CRF while shortening the separation further.

Continue shifting the gradient window upward at constant slope, now reaching the maximum endpoint. The previous shifts preserved full resolution, so this may further shorten elution while maintaining CRF 1.000.

Raise only the starting organic fraction to narrow the gradient window and accelerate elution. The shallower slope may improve resolution, although the earliest pair could become sensitive to reduced initial retention.
Use the improved first-pair resolution margin to test one temperature step higher. This should accelerate the last peak while checking whether the critical pair remains above 1.5.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to seek faster elution at the current successful temperature. Monitor the first pair closely because its proximity to the solvent front may offset the resolution benefit of a shallower gradient.

Restore the starting fraction that preserved early-pair retention and test one temperature step above injection 13. This locates the temperature limit for the fastest fully resolved method found so far; injection 13 remains the fallback if resolution drops below 1.5.

Test whether lower temperature restores the early-pair selectivity lost at a starting fraction of 0.35. This completes the local starting-solvent boundary check; injection 13 remains the fastest method with maximum CRF.

Reduce the endpoint one step from injection 13 to increase the critical pair’s resolution margin while keeping a short separation. The maximum CRF is already achieved; this tests a potentially more robust alternative to the fastest successful method.

Lower the starting fraction to move the earliest peaks away from the solvent front and test a nearby fully resolved alternative. Compare its critical-pair resolution with injections 13 and 17; injection 13 remains the fastest maximum-CRF method.

Lower temperature one step from injection 17 to improve the critical pair’s resolution margin while retaining a short, maximum-CRF separation. Injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved method; this tests a less marginal alternative.

Lower the endpoint one step to test whether a gentler gradient provides additional early-pair resolution while keeping all peaks well within 10 minutes. The maximum score is already secured, and injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved method found.

Raise temperature one step from injection 20 to shorten elution while using its early-pair resolution margin. This tests a nearby maximum-CRF alternative; injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved method found.

Test a lower starting fraction near the successful short-gradient methods to retain the earliest peaks farther from the solvent front while targeting full resolution. The maximum CRF is already secured, with injection 13 still the fastest fully resolved method found.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 22 to shorten final elution while targeting full resolution. The neighboring successful methods suggest sufficient early-pair resolution margin to retain CRF 1.000.

Raise temperature one step from injection 22 to shorten elution while targeting full resolution with the earliest peaks farther from the solvent front. Injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated method attaining the maximum CRF of 1.000.

Test a final nearby method expected to preserve full resolution while retaining the earliest peaks farther from the solvent front. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 13 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method, with the last peak at 2.58 minutes.
